tldr: By decoupling physics-based trajectory generation from high-quality Movie Render Queue rendering into two stages, this system reliably and automatically generates large-scale multi-view video from Unreal Engine with actions and frames perfectly synchronized.
hero_caption: Overall view of the end-to-end data generation workflow. It integrates asset curation, distributed scheduling, Stage I physics trajectory generation, Stage II offline MRQ rendering, and output management with upload under a unified set of reliability safeguards.
overview:
Interactive "world models" that predict future visual changes in response to user or agent actions are rapidly gaining attention. However, training them requires large-scale data where actions and visual transitions are strictly synchronized frame by frame, which is extremely difficult to collect from ordinary real-world video. In real-world footage, the underlying control inputs are typically unknown.

To address this, the authors propose a scalable pipeline that leverages Unreal Engine's (UE) rich ecosystem of 3D assets to synthesize action-conditioned multi-view video. The biggest hurdle here lies in the game engine's execution model. Simulating realistic collisions and gravity requires real-time physics engine execution, but exporting high-quality video requires temporal and spatial supersampling via Movie Render Queue (MRQ) (accumulating multiple render passes). These two requirements cannot naturally coexist within the same engine process.

To overcome this challenge, the authors designed an approach that cleanly decouples generation into "Stage I" for physics simulation and "Stage II" for deterministically replaying the trajectory file to perform high-quality offline rendering. Furthermore, to run a 200-GPU cluster efficiently, they integrated cache-aware task partitioning, automated quality filtering, and partial-output recovery when processes fail.

Operating across 25 servers (200 NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPUs in total), the system successfully produced 2,691 hours of 1080p video and 6,076 hours of 720p video across 429 levels and 40 humanoid characters. It serves as the foundation data pipeline for the state-of-the-art world model EchoWM.
contributions: Established an action-conditioned multi-view video generation pipeline with perfectly synchronized actions, poses, and cameras by decoupling physics simulation (Stage I) from high-quality offline rendering (Stage II) via an intermediate trajectory representation.
Achieved high-throughput parallel execution on a 200-GPU cluster using fixed level-pool assignments that maximize shader and texture cache locality, combined with node-local slot scheduling.

Built an operationally reliable system resilient to the instability of third-party assets, incorporating low-resolution pre-screening, automated aesthetic and luminance filtering, and partial-output recovery upon crashes.
Produced over 8,700 total hours of high-quality action-conditioned video using 429 curated levels and 40 humanoid characters selected from 2,384 commercial asset packs.

sections.heading: Why Build Pretraining Data for World Models in a Game Engine?
sections.summary: Training interactive video world models requires strict temporal alignment between actions and frames, which real-world video struggles to provide. This study presents an infrastructure for stably generating action-labeled multi-view video across a 200-GPU cluster using diverse Unreal Engine assets.
sections.details:
Recent years have seen rapid progress in interactive generative world models like Genie, GameNGen, and EchoWM. Scaling these models requires not just diverse visual appearances, but massive volumes of data where control actions and 6-DoF camera movements are temporally aligned with visual scene changes down to the exact frame.

While web videos are visually diverse, an operator's control inputs and true 6-DoF camera poses cannot be observed directly and must be estimated. On the other hand, gameplay footage provides explicit inputs but remains tightly constrained to specific game environments. As a result, recent world models increasingly rely on synthetic 3D environments.

This paper focuses directly on establishing a synthetic data production component using Unreal Engine (UE). When attempting this in UE, running real-time physics (collision detection and gravity) and running high-quality cinematic offline rendering via Movie Render Queue (MRQ) are fundamentally incompatible within the engine's execution architecture. To resolve this, the authors designed a two-stage workflow: Stage I generates trajectories, and Stage II replays and renders them.

In addition, because third-party commercial assets vary widely in quality and frequently crash the engine, the authors integrated cache-aware scheduling, quality screening, and partial recovery mechanisms, building a production-grade system on a cluster of 200 RTX 5090 GPUs.

sections.heading: The Frontier of Evolving World Models and Data Generation
sections.summary: Recent world models have shifted from simple next-frame prediction to interactive generation conditioned on actions and camera controls. Consequently, building data engines that combine synthetic environments, gameplay, and real-world video has become a core pillar of research.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Interactive Generative World Models
Video generation models have advanced to the point of generating long multi-minute sequences and supporting real-time interaction. Notable examples include WorldPlay for long-term geometric consistency, SANA-WM for explicit camera control, DreamX-World for multi-environment navigation, and Cosmos and EchoWM for integrating multimodal inputs like actions. As these models become more sophisticated, the precision of camera geometry and action labels used during training increasingly dictates their performance.

### 2.2 Data Construction for Interactive World Models
To fuel these models, platforms like Matrix-Game 3.0 and DreamX-World build data engines combining UE synthetic data, AAA gameplay logs, and real-world video. Furthermore, systematic filtering and data curation have become widely recognized as essential, as seen in SpatialVID's spatial annotations for real video and Cosmos's data pipeline.

This paper shares that data-centric perspective but executes its entire simulation inside UE. While this eliminates estimation errors in spatial coordinates and control inputs, it introduces new systems challenges: dealing with asset-specific bugs, collision anomalies, and broken lighting inherent to third-party 3D assets.

sections.heading: Data Generation Overview: Multi-View and a Two-Stage Pipeline
sections.summary: Each sample consists of a 1-minute trajectory (1,800 frames) paired with 9 discrete actions and 5 synchronized camera views. The core of this methodology is separating processing into Stage I for physics simulation and Stage II for high-quality offline rendering.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Action-Conditioned Multi-View Data
A single data sample consists of synchronized video captured from five cameras as a character navigates a 3D level, paired with per-frame control signals. The action space consists of 9 discrete inputs: forward, backward, left, right, four diagonals, and IDLE. A standard trajectory records 1,800 frames (1 minute at 30 fps), with character poses, camera states, and key inputs temporally aligned for every frame.

### 3.2 Why Decouple into Two Stages?
This is the core architectural insight. Real-time physics simulation and offline high-quality rendering impose fundamentally incompatible demands on the engine:

- Stage I (Physics-Based Trajectory Generation): Runs in Play In Editor (PIE) mode, allowing UE's physics engine to resolve slopes, gravity, and collision in real time. Visual fidelity is unnecessary here; the focus is solely on recording character states, camera trajectories, and action inputs into an intermediate file.
- Stage II (Trajectory Replay and Offline Rendering): Launches a clean UE process, loads the trajectory file from Stage I to reposition the character and cameras frame by frame, and renders them offline using Movie Render Queue (MRQ).

In short, Stage I determines "what happened," while Stage II handles "how beautifully it is rendered." By inserting this intermediate trajectory contract, the pipeline achieves both physical plausibility and cinematic rendering quality.

captions.F1: Sample of generated multi-view video. Five camera perspectives—top-down overhead view, bottom-row third-person follow view, center first-person view, and left/right side views—are captured in complete temporal synchronization.

sections.heading: Curating and Preparing Heterogeneous 3D Assets
sections.summary: From 2,384 asset packs gathered on the Fab store, 429 production levels were selected after renderability tests and automated quality scoring. In addition, 40 humanoid characters underwent collision and animation calibration.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Asset Preparation and Setup
Scene assets acquired from the Fab marketplace are stored in central object storage and synced to the local SSDs of compute nodes as needed. UE performs frequent random file reads, making direct loading from network storage prohibitively slow. Global configuration files normalize directory structures and exclude preview showcase levels or unmanageable open-world scenes unsuited for automation.

For characters, bounding boxes are computed from meshes to automatically size capsule collision shapes, and animations are bound to the 9 discrete actions. For meshes with extreme horizontal proportions (such as a bat with outstretched wings), capsule height diverges from visual height and corrupts camera framing; the system handles this by referencing actual visual height for camera framing calculations.

### 4.2 Two-Stage Pre-Production Screening
To prevent broken levels from wasting production cluster resources, a rigorous two-step screening is performed:

- Renderability Checks: Five 10-second clips at 540p are rendered to visually inspect for startup crashes, missing walkable navmesh, invisible collision meshes causing floating characters, or floor clipping.
- Visual Quality Filtering: Using tools adapted from SpatialVID, an image quality model measures aesthetic score ($aes$) and average luminance ($lum$). Twenty 10-second clips are generated per level; only levels where at least 25% of frames satisfy $aes > 5.5$ and $25 < lum < 140$ (neither underexposed nor blown out) are retained for production.

### 4.3 Dataset Scale and Diversity
Ultimately, 429 levels and 40 characters were retained. Levels are well-balanced across historical/fantasy, sci-fi, nature/landscape, and urban/architecture genres, each accounting for roughly 20–30%. In the action distribution, diagonal movement, reversing, and strafing account for 46.6% of frames, ensuring diverse locomotion rather than monotonous forward walking.

sections.heading: Distributed Scheduling Designed to Maximize Cache Locality
sections.summary: The system employs a three-tier architecture: a central allocator, node-local schedulers, and an independent uploader. Assigning levels to nodes as fixed pools cuts shader compilation and cold-start overhead by more than half.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Distributed Operational Architecture
The cluster operates via coordination between a central task allocator, node-local schedulers running on each machine, and output uploaders. Tracking the state of hundreds of render slots centrally would introduce communication bottlenecks, so high-frequency process management—such as process spawning, termination, and retries—is handled entirely by the node-local schedulers.

### 5.2 Cache-Aware Task Scheduling
When UE opens a scene for the first time, massive shader compilation and texture caching occur, easily causing cold-start times exceeding 10 minutes. If every node grabbed scenes at random, this initialization cost would recur continuously and decimate throughput.

To solve this, the level list is partitioned into fixed pools matching the number of nodes, ensuring each node repeatedly renders only its assigned pool of levels. Once a pass is completed, the order is shuffled and repeated. Because spawn points and action trajectories are randomized on every run, the resulting videos remain distinct even within the same level. This strategy reduced re-visit rendering time to less than half of cold-start times.

### 5.3 Slot-Level Concurrency
Each node contains 8 RTX 5090 GPUs running multiple concurrent slots (UE processes). Because a single UE process cannot saturate a GPU due to asset loading and I/O stalls, sharing each GPU across multiple processes maximizes cluster throughput. Each slot runs under an isolated virtual display (X11) environment to prevent interference.

sections.heading: Stage I: Generating Natural Locomotion on a Physics Engine
sections.summary: A state machine driven by UE frame callbacks achieves fully automated physics-based navigation. It incorporates point-of-interest guidance, automatic unstuck maneuvers, and smooth five-view camera controls that avoid obstacles.
sections.details:
### 6.1 Frame-Driven Control and Spawning
When scripting automation in UE, blocking sleep loops halt the engine's internal frame updates entirely. This pipeline instead registers a callback invoked every frame: a state machine checks the current state, submits the next control input, and immediately returns control to the engine. This allows falling, step navigation, and wall collisions to resolve naturally through standard UE physics.

Character spawning is equally critical. Candidate locations are chosen from level start points or near objects, characters are spawned mid-air, and the system waits until gravity grounds them stably. If a character fails to settle within a timeout, it is resampled.

### 6.2 Action Sampling and Unstuck Logic
Switching actions randomly every frame causes unnatural character jitter. The system uses temporal holding, maintaining a chosen action for a randomized number of frames to produce smooth movement.

- POI (Point of Interest) Guidance: Pure random walks tend to linger around the initial spawn point. Without altering the underlying action probabilities, the character's orientation is gently guided toward scene objects (POIs) to encourage broader exploration.
- Unstuck Detection: If movement input is active but position remains nearly unchanged over time, the system flags the character as stuck and initiates an escape turn maneuver. If that fails, it triggers a respawn at a new location.

### 6.3 Multi-View Camera Trajectories and Occlusion Avoidance
Once character movement is determined, trajectories for five cameras (rear follow, left, right, top-down, and first-person) are calculated. External cameras easily clip into walls, so raycasts are fired from the character to each camera position, pulling the camera forward if an obstruction is hit. To avoid jarring camera jumps, asymmetric smoothing is applied: the camera retracts quickly upon collision and recovers slowly once cleared, preserving visual stability.

sections.heading: Stage II: High-Quality Offline Rendering with MRQ
sections.summary: To eliminate the aliasing artifacts unavoidable in real-time screen capture, the pipeline adopts cinematic-grade Movie Render Queue (MRQ). It deterministically replays recorded trajectories, disables unwanted cinematic sequences, and forces texture residency before rendering.
sections.details:
### 7.1 Why MRQ Over Real-Time Capture?
The team initially tested capturing the screen directly during Stage I (SceneCapture). However, in headless scripted environments, temporal anti-aliasing was unstable and left severe aliasing artifacts across geometry edges.

They switched to Movie Render Queue (MRQ). Because MRQ is an offline renderer free from real-time constraints, it applies extensive temporal and spatial supersampling per frame (rendering multiple sub-frames and accumulating them). This produces pristine, temporally stable footage. While MRQ is fundamentally incompatible with real-time physics—because it rolls back simulation and evaluates sub-frames—recording deterministic trajectories in Stage I unlocks MRQ's full rendering potential.

### 7.2 Rendering with MRQ and Practical Workarounds
In Stage II, the exact capsule position, rotation, and scale recorded in Stage I are reconstructed along a sequence timeline. Doing this reliably required several operational workarounds:

- Strict Transform Reconstruction: Failing to record scale causes character sizes to reset upon replay, and mismatching the capsule center and mesh origin offset causes characters to float or sink into floors. The system strictly applies the exact transforms captured by the engine.
- Scene Sanitization: Commercial assets often contain auto-playing promotional cinematic sequences upon loading. If triggered, these take over the camera. The system scans levels beforehand and automatically strips out sequence actors.
- Forcing Texture Residency: UE's texture streaming prioritizes interactive performance, often displaying blurry, low-resolution textures during the first few frames. The pipeline enlarges streaming pools and forces high-resolution textures into memory prior to offline rendering, guaranteeing crisp quality from frame zero.

Image sequences exported by MRQ are immediately encoded into video files, and the raw image frames are deleted promptly to conserve storage.

sections.heading: Operational Practices to Keep a 200-GPU Cluster Running 24/7
sections.summary: Built on the assumption that crashes will occur, the system ensures high operational reliability through loosely coupled log monitoring for partial recovery, asynchronous uploads, and monitoring for GPU state desynchronization between host and containers.
sections.details:
### 8.1 Artifact Management and Inspection Tools
Output directories follow a hierarchical `scene/level/instance/trajectory` structure, combining node IDs and timestamps to prevent overwrites. For data quality inspection, a lightweight UI tool (Figure 5) was developed to simultaneously step through synchronized 5-view videos, 3D trajectory paths, and the exact keyboard inputs for each frame.

### 8.2 Partial Recovery via Loosely Coupled Log Monitoring
UE processes occasionally crash without warning. Tightly binding the scheduler and UE via direct APIs would cause cascading failures. Instead, the scheduler monitors simple progress log markers that UE appends after completing each trajectory. If an entire batch fails midway, completed trajectories with valid markers and video files are salvaged, while corrupt partial files are discarded, minimizing wasted GPU time.

### 8.3 Asynchronous Uploads and Failure Snapshots
To prevent cloud uploads from blocking GPU rendering, uploaders run as independent daemon processes. Safeguards ensure files are only transferred after write activity has stopped for a set duration, avoiding corrupt transfers of actively encoding videos. When errors occur, a failure snapshot containing logs, exit codes, and GPU states is saved for post-mortem analysis.

### 8.4 Cluster Health Monitoring and Auto-Recovery
One of the most insidious failure modes was GPU loss inside Docker containers while the host system still reported the GPU as healthy. External watchdog scripts detect this container-host divergence, automatically rebuilding containers and restarting schedulers to maintain uninterrupted 24/7 production.

sections.heading: Is Visual Quality Really the Right Proxy? Current Limitations
sections.summary: How perceptual metrics like aesthetic scores translate to world model pretraining efficiency remains an open question. Furthermore, the current action space is limited to character-centric locomotion, leaving complex interactions like jumping and manipulation for future work.
sections.details:
### Trade-offs in Data Generation
This pipeline does not simply optimize for cinematic beauty. It balances action diversity, physical validity, visual fidelity, and computational cost. For instance, aggressive exploration guidance reduces behavioral diversity, while overly strict visual filters discard structurally varied environments.

### Perceptual Quality Proxies and Downstream Performance
The current aesthetic and luminance thresholds successfully filter out pitch-black scenes and gross rendering failures. However, images that look pleasing to humans do not necessarily represent the best data for learning physical world dynamics. Filtering may inadvertently discard geometrically valuable scenes simply because they look rough, making the downstream impact of curation metrics an important area for future study.

### Action Coordinates and Repertoire Limitations
The current implementation uses a character-centric coordinate frame, though camera-centric control (e.g., moving deeper into the scene relative to a fixed view) is also being tested. Furthermore, actions are currently restricted to basic locomotion: walking, running, and turning. Expanding to richer interactions—such as jumping, vaulting over obstacles, and manipulating objects—remains an active challenge.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Synthetic Data Infrastructure for the World Model Era
sections.summary: This work establishes a robust pipeline for generating fully synchronized, action-conditioned multi-view video from large-scale Unreal Engine assets. Generating roughly 8,700 hours of video across 200 GPUs, it forms the data backbone for the EchoWM world model.
sections.details:
This paper presents a large-scale Unreal Engine synthetic data generation pipeline designed for pretraining world models. The fundamental conflict between real-time physics and high-quality offline rendering is resolved through a two-stage architecture: Stage I for physics trajectory generation, and Stage II for offline MRQ replay rendering.

Deployed across 25 nodes (200 RTX 5090 GPUs), the system integrates asset pre-screening, locality-aware pool scheduling, failure recovery for partial outputs, and automated cluster health checks. Curating 429 production levels from 2,384 commercial asset packs, it achieved 2,691 hours of 1080p and 6,076 hours of 720p video generation.

Rather than introducing a new predictive model, this report focuses on the underlying data production infrastructure. The operational insights and failure mitigations detailed here offer valuable practical guidance for scaling synthetic data production for interactive world models and robotics.

takeaways: Do not force real-time physics simulation and offline high-quality rendering into a single engine process; decoupling them via an intermediate trajectory file is the winning pattern in Unreal Engine.

In large-scale Unreal Engine batch workloads, cold starts from shader compilation are the primary bottleneck; cache-locality scheduling with fixed level pools per node cuts rendering times by more than half.

Automating third-party commercial 3D assets will inevitably trigger crashes; implementing loosely coupled log monitoring with partial recovery (salvaging completed clips prior to a crash) is essential for maintaining cluster uptime.
limitations: Quantitative verification is still lacking on whether human perceptual filters (aesthetic and luminance scores) genuinely benefit downstream world models in learning physical dynamics.
The action space is restricted to 9 planar locomotion and turning states, lacking complex interactions such as jumping, climbing, or object manipulation.
Initial asset screening (detecting startup crashes and collision bugs) still incurs human labor costs through visual inspection of low-resolution preview clips.
